Apache Ignite is not built on top of a relational database. Its docs (Ignite 3.1, checked Oct 2026) call it 'a distributed database for high-performance computing with in-memory speed'. It has its own in-memory storage and optional native persistence (partition files plus a write-ahead log) and a SQL engine. precise_version: Apache Ignite is a distributed in-memory database with its own storage engine, SQL support and optional native persistence; it can sit in front of an RDBMS as a cache, but it is not built on one.

precise_version: Upsert syntax differs: PostgreSQL uses INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE; MySQL uses INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE (REPLACE INTO also works but deletes the old row and inserts a new one).

InnoDB does not rebalance the B+ tree on every delete. It delete-marks the row and a background purge removes it later. Cheap for small values, not always. redis.conf: DEL is a blocking deletion and, for large objects, 'the server can block for a long time (even seconds)'. That is why UNLINK and the lazyfree options free memory on a background thread.

B+ tree databases do not rebalance on every single delete. InnoDB delete-marks the row and its index records and purges them later in the background. It merges a page with a neighbour only when the page falls below MERGE_THRESHOLD (default 50% full). Point deletes cost roughly what an update costs, not 'pathetically slow'. Batching expiry cleanup is still sensible: it is a range delete driven by the expired_at index instead of many scattered writes. But 'never delete per key on disk' over-states it; the soft-delete UPDATE also rewrites the row and the expired_at index entry.
precise_version: On disk-based B+ tree stores, prefer batched cleanup of expired rows, but single deletes are not catastrophic: engines like InnoDB delete-mark rows, purge them in the background and merge pages only when they get under-full.

This is the classic (pre-6.0) algorithm: sample 20 random keys with an expire, delete the expired ones, repeat if more than 25% were expired. Redis 6.0 (RC1, Dec 2019) 'rewrote' the active expire cycle and made its effort tunable. Current source (Redis unstable, checked Oct 2026) still uses ACTIVE_EXPIRE_CYCLE_KEYS_PER_LOOP 20 as the base batch (scaled up by active-expire-effort). But it walks the expires table with a persistent scan cursor instead of picking random keys, and repeats while more than ~10% of what it checked was stale. The idea (check a small batch, keep going only while many are expired, stay within a time budget) is unchanged.
precise_version: Classic Redis checked 20 random keys with a TTL per round; since Redis 6.0 the cycle scans the TTL table incrementally in batches (20 keys at default effort) and keeps going while more than about 10% are stale, within a CPU time budget.

The 25% repeat threshold is the pre-6.0 rule. In current Redis (source checked Oct 2026) the loop repeats while expired/sampled exceeds ACTIVE_EXPIRE_CYCLE_ACCEPTABLE_STALE = 10% (lower with higher active-expire-effort), and a time limit also ends the cycle. redis.conf: the default effort 'will try to avoid having more than ten percent of expired keys still in memory'.

The arithmetic matches the classic 25% rule. Under the current (Redis 6.0+) rule, a batch with 15% stale keys is above the 10% acceptable-stale threshold, so the cycle would keep going (time budget permitting).

Redis executes commands on one main thread, but it is not true that no other threads run. redis.conf: 'Redis is mostly single threaded, however there are certain threaded operations such as UNLINK, slow I/O accesses and other things that are performed on side threads'. Threaded I/O exists since 6.0. Memory of expired keys can be freed on a background thread (lazyfree-lazy-expire, default no). The conclusion (keep work on the main thread short) is right.
precise_version: Redis runs commands on a single main thread, so it keeps expiry work short; background threads exist for lazy freeing (UNLINK/lazyfree), file I/O and optional network I/O.

note: The bound is on the share of keys-with-TTL that are expired but not yet removed, not on total memory, and it is probabilistic. With current Redis the default target is about 10% ('avoid having more than ten percent of expired keys still in memory'), not 20-25%.

An open WebSocket does not by itself prove the user is online. If the network drops (Wi-Fi lost, phone sleeps, NAT entry expires), no close frame or TCP FIN may arrive, and the server can keep a dead connection open for a long time. That is why RFC 6455 defines Ping/Pong frames: 'A Ping frame may serve either as a keepalive or as a means to verify that the remote endpoint is still responsive'. Real systems use ping/pong or TCP keepalive with timeouts. The heartbeat moves into the protocol layer rather than disappearing. What WhatsApp Web does internally is not public.
precise_version: A WebSocket removes the need for HTTP heartbeat calls, but liveness still needs WebSocket ping/pong (or TCP keepalive) with a timeout, because a dropped connection may not be noticed otherwise.
